extracted.intended_audience: researchers, journal editors, research-integrity officers, and the interested scientific public
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and community-sourced criteria for identifying, reporting, and evaluating possible research misconduct in published biomedical papers (image manipulation, duplicated figures, improper controls, redundant publication) and for how institutions/journals should respond. Emphasizes technical signs, patterns across a corpus, and procedural/ethical expectations for investigations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Image/figure manipulation and duplication
rubrics_metrics.description: Re-use or manipulation of images across figures or papers (e.g., duplicated bands, pasted/added cells, same control images used for different conditions).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples cited include “re-use of beta-actin control blots for different conditions,” duplications of the same figure across papers, and cases where apoptotic cells have been added. Community reviewers note that figure duplications and manipulations are relatively easy to spot and list multiple paper examples; repeat occurrences across many papers strengthen suspicion of intentional manipulation rather than honest error.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specific forensic signs in blot/figure images
rubrics_metrics.description: Technical irregularities visible in images (missing lane backgrounds, identical control values repeated across papers, splicing artifacts, inconsistent band spacing or intensity distributions).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Commenters give forensic cues such as identical MDA values across papers, apparent splicing (a band/background mismatch), missing lane background in one lane, or band intensity distributions that don't match. These observable inconsistencies are offered as concrete evidence to flag figures for closer inspection or forensic analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proper use and reporting of Western blot loading controls
rubrics_metrics.description: Loading controls should correspond to the specific gel/blot and not be reused across different experiments without disclosure; when probing same blot for multiple proteins this must be documented.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Discussion notes that although a single blot can be cut and reprobed for several proteins, this should be documented on the films; routinely reusing a single loading control image across different gels/conditions (a “universal loading control”) is a red flag. Journals/editors and investigators should check whether the loading control matches the presented protein blots and whether reuse is justified and declared.

rubrics_metrics.name: Flow cytometry (FC) data integrity and presentation standards
rubrics_metrics.description: FC data must be properly acquired and presented (correct gating, doublet discrimination, appropriate voltage settings, use of log vs linear scales where standard, and correct controls).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Commenters flag examples of ungated data, altered FL1/FL2 voltages to produce desired populations, missing doublet discrimination, and improper scale use (e.g., BrdU acquisition). Critiques stress that altering voltages/gating post-hoc to produce desired results or presenting ungated populations as controls undermines validity; experts should evaluate raw FC files and acquisition details.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish honest error from intentional misconduct
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess whether anomalies stem from isolated honest mistakes (e.g., accidental figure duplication) or from systematic/intentional fabrication or falsification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Several commenters argue that a few duplications might be honest errors in high-volume publishing, but repeated duplications across many papers (and manipulations like added cells) point toward intentional misconduct. Frequency, pattern, and the nature of edits (substantive additions vs accidental repeats) inform intent assessments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pattern-based review of an author's corpus
rubrics_metrics.description: Investigations should look across an author's publication record for recurring problems (figure reuse, identical controls, repeated conclusions across many papers), not only single-paper anomalies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The blog and commenters compiled lists (14→22+ papers) showing repeated irregularities across years and different co-authors; such patterns (e.g., the same control values across multiple papers) provide stronger evidence than isolated issues and justify broader institutional or journal review.

rubrics_metrics.name: Redundant and 'salami' publication
rubrics_metrics.description: Publishing multiple papers with only minor differences (same system/results repeated with different compounds or slight tweaks) can constitute redundant or salami publication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Commenters define the difference (major overlap = redundant publication; minor overlap = salami slicing) and point to flowcharts (e.g., COPE flowchart) and editorial queries that ask authors about related submissions. Editors should ask for disclosure of similar or related submissions and investigate excessive overlapping content.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unusually high publication rates as a red flag
rubrics_metrics.description: Extremely high numbers of publications in a short time (e.g., multiple papers per month) can indicate 'assembly-line' production of low-quality or potentially fraudulent papers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Discussion notes that 600 papers or 3+ papers/month is suspicious for a non-clinical researcher; while clinicians may publish many case reports, prolific output inconsistent with grant/support levels or laboratory capacity should prompt scrutiny of data provenance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preservation and review of original/raw data
rubrics_metrics.description: Raw/original files (original blots, flow cytometry FCS files, uncropped images) must be preserved and reviewed to confirm image integrity and determine if alterations occurred.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Commenters assert that "original files can never tell lies" and recommend inspecting originals to detect manipulations. Journals and institutions should request raw data during inquiries; lack of raw data or inability to provide originals is itself a concern.

rubrics_metrics.name: Journal/editor responsibilities (corrections, expressions of concern, retractions)
rubrics_metrics.description: Journals should investigate flagged issues, request explanations and raw data, issue corrections or retractions when warranted, and require disclosure of related publications.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples referenced include published corrections (e.g., Cell) and calls for retraction; editors are expected to follow COPE guidance and to act when evidence supports correction or retraction. Community reporting to journals is encouraged when irregularities are found.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reporting channels and involvement of oversight bodies (ORI/government)
rubrics_metrics.description: Serious allegations, especially where federal funding is involved, should be reported to institutional Research Integrity Officers and, if appropriate, to external bodies like the Office of Research Integrity (ORI).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Commenters describe emailing MD Anderson's Research Integrity Officer and the institution's president; note that government oversight exists for federally funded work. They recommend involving external bodies when institutional conflict of interest is suspected or when internal inquiry is inadequate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Institutional conflict of interest and need for impartial inquiry
rubrics_metrics.description: Institutions investigating their own faculty may have conflicts (embarrassment, funding, IP); impartial external review is recommended when conflicts are likely.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Multiple comments stress that an internal inquiry can be biased and propose external, third-party investigations (or government oversight) to ensure credibility. If an internal inquiry clears an author, an external inquiry should be available to validate findings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transparency and timeliness of institutional responses
rubrics_metrics.description: Institutions should communicate about investigations in a timely and reasonably transparent way to maintain public trust and protect research integrity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Blog and commenters criticize lack of public response from MD Anderson and urge institutions to inform stakeholders; blanket silence or delays fuel suspicion and public criticism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid ad hominem and preserve constructive discourse
rubrics_metrics.description: Community discussions about misconduct should avoid ad hominem attacks and abusive comments, focusing on evidence and methods to improve scientific processes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The post explicitly requests readers to "Please refrain from ad hominem attacks, as they undermine this community’s attempts to improve our understanding of the scientific process." Moderation (unapproving abusive comments) is used to maintain constructive debate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration of lab culture and working conditions as contributing factors
rubrics_metrics.description: Extremely demanding lab environments, poor supervision, or exploitative practices can foster mistakes or misconduct and should be examined in investigations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Commenters recount long work hours, intense pressure to publish, and alleged coercive lab leadership; such contextual factors should be part of investigations and institutional oversight.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conflict of interest disclosures and committee memberships
rubrics_metrics.description: Authors’ and institutional officers' potential conflicts (e.g., committee roles, collaborations, commercial interests) should be transparent and examined in misconduct inquiries.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Commenters question whether committee memberships and commercial ties were disclosed and whether they conformed to MD Anderson policies; undeclared conflicts can undermine the credibility of investigations and should be checked.

rubrics_metrics.name: Community/whistleblower role and evidence compilation
rubrics_metrics.description: Independent bloggers, post-publication peer review, and whistleblowers can play a key role in compiling evidence and bringing possible misconduct to light.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The post documents how blogs (Abnormal Science, md-anderson-cc) listed problematic papers and images; community compilation of examples and technical analyses can prompt formal investigations but should be accompanied by careful documentation and avoidance of defamatory claims.
